jd.m1.1.q: 1. x has shape [7, 4096] and W has shape [4096, 1024]. What shape does x @ W get?
jd.m1.1.e: The last axis of x (4096) must match the first axis of W. It is replaced by W’s second axis: [7, 1024]. The 7 rows are processed independently.
jd.m1.2.q: 2. Two vectors have dot product 0. What does that mean?
jd.m1.2.e: a·b = |a||b|cos θ. Zero means cos θ = 0, that is 90°. The same direction gives a large positive value, the opposite direction a negative one.
jd.m1.2.o1: They point in the same direction
jd.m1.2.o2: They are perpendicular: one says nothing about the other
jd.m1.2.o4: One of them must be the zero vector
jd.m1.3.q: 3. Three linear layers are stacked with no activation function in between. What can they express?
jd.m1.3.e: x @ W1 @ W2 @ W3 = x @ (W1 W2 W3). The product of the matrices is a matrix. Only with a non-linearity in between does each layer add anything.
jd.m1.3.o2: Exactly the same thing as a single linear layer
jd.m1.3.o3: Nothing, the output is always zero
jd.m1.4.q: 4. You add 10 to every logit before softmax. What happens to the probabilities?
jd.m1.4.e: Softmax depends only on the differences between logits. A constant in all of them cancels out.
jd.m1.4.o2: The largest one takes over completely
jd.m1.5.q: 5. A dense model processes a token. How many of the weights in an MLP layer are used in the calculation?
jd.m1.5.e: All weights are multiplied every time. The activation function zeroes activations, not weights. The activations are what differ between tokens.
jd.m1.5.o1: Only the ones that belong to the topic
jd.m1.5.o2: About half, the rest is zeroed by the activation function
jd.m2.1.q: 1. What decides how a text is split into tokens?
jd.m2.1.e: The tokenizer is a fixed, separate component. The same text always gives the same ids.
jd.m2.1.o2: The tokenizer’s merges, fixed before the model was trained
jd.m2.2.q: 2. What does a chat template do?
jd.m2.2.e: The model only sees one long token sequence. The template inserts special tokens that mark where each role starts and ends.
jd.m2.2.o2: Picks which system prompt to use
jd.m2.2.o3: Turns the list of messages into a single string with special tokens for the roles
jd.m2.3.q: 3. Why is embedding called a lookup rather than a matrix multiplication?
jd.m2.3.e: x = E[ids]. No arithmetic, just copying rows. The table is learned, though, just like every other weight.
jd.m2.3.o1: The table is too big to multiply
jd.m2.3.o2: Each id simply picks out a row from the table
jd.m2.4.q: 4. A prompt is 2,000 words of Swedish text. Roughly how many tokens is that most likely?
jd.m2.4.e: Swedish words are often split into several tokens. Count on well over one token per word, plus punctuation.
jd.m3.1.e: The original had an encoder and a decoder. Decoder-only models like GPT and Llama have just one stack with a causal mask.
jd.m3.1.o1: The model has only MLP layers, no attention layers
jd.m3.1.o2: The model keeps only the generating half of the original transformer: a stack where each token looks backwards
jd.m3.1.o3: The model can only read text, not write it
jd.m3.2.q: 2. Why does the stream have the same shape [T, 4096] after every block?
jd.m3.2.e: The output of one block must fit as the input of the next, and x + contribution requires the same shape.
jd.m3.2.o1: It is a coincidence in Llama’s configuration
jd.m3.2.o2: So that blocks can be stacked and contributions added to the stream
jd.m3.2.o3: Because the GPU can only handle one shape
jd.m3.2.o4: It does change in every block
jd.m3.3.q: 3. Why is a final RMSNorm needed before the LM head in Llama?
jd.m3.3.e: The blocks read normalized copies, but the stream itself grows. It is normalized once before it is turned into logits.
jd.m3.3.o1: Because the LM head has no weights
jd.m3.3.o2: Because pre-norm never normalizes the stream itself along the way
jd.m3.4.q: 4. How many weight matrices are there in one layer of Llama-3-8B (not counting the norm vectors)?
jd.m3.4.e: Wq, Wk, Wv and Wo in attention, W_gate, W_up and W_down in the MLP. On top of that, two norm vectors of 4096.
jd.m3.5.q: 5. What happens to x in the line x = x + Attention(RMSNorm(x))?
jd.m3.5.e: RMSNorm is applied to a copy. The stream itself changes only through the addition.
jd.m3.5.o1: x is normalized and replaced by the attention result
jd.m3.5.o2: A normalized copy of x goes into attention, and the result is added to the unnormalized x
jd.m3.5.o3: x is multiplied by the attention result
jd.m3.5.o4: x is passed through attention twice
jd.m3.6.q: 6. Which statement about the MLP is correct?
jd.m3.6.e: Exchange between tokens happens only in attention, in the P · V step.
jd.m3.6.o1: It lets tokens read from each other
jd.m3.6.o2: It processes each token separately, with the same weights for all tokens
jd.m3.6.o3: It has different weights for each token
jd.m3.6.o4: It is only used in the first layer
jd.m3.7.q: 7. Where in the block do tokens exchange information with each other?
jd.m3.7.e: The MLP, the normalization and the addition work on each position separately. Attention is the only place where one position reads from others.
jd.m3.8.q: 8. What shape does K have in one layer of Llama-3-8B for T tokens, after splitting into heads?
jd.m3.8.e: 8 KV heads of 128 dimensions each. Q has 32 heads; four query heads share each KV head (GQA).
jd.m3.9.q: 9. What does the causal mask guarantee?
jd.m3.9.e: Scores against later positions are set to −∞ and become 0 after softmax. So nothing changes for an old position when new tokens arrive.
jd.m3.9.o1: That position i is never affected by later positions
jd.m3.9.o2: That all heads look at different tokens
jd.m3.9.o3: That K and V have the same scale
jd.m3.9.o4: That the model sees the whole prompt at once
jd.m3.10.q: 10. How does a layer update the residual stream?
jd.m3.10.e: x = x + contribution. The shape [T, 4096] is the same through all layers.
jd.m3.10.o1: It replaces the stream with its result
jd.m3.10.o2: It multiplies the stream by its result
jd.m3.10.o3: It adds its result to the stream
jd.m3.10.o4: It puts its result alongside, so the stream gets wider
jd.m3.11.e: The rotation happens inside each attention layer, on Q and K. V and the residual stream are not touched.
jd.m3.11.o1: Adds a position vector to the embedding
jd.m3.11.o2: Rotates Q and K so that their dot product depends on the distance between positions
jd.m3.11.o3: Sorts the tokens into the right order
jd.m4.1.q: 1. How many numbers do the logits contain for one position in Llama-3-8B?
jd.m4.1.e: One number per token in the vocabulary.
jd.m4.1.o4: As many as there are tokens in the prompt
jd.m4.2.q: 2. What does temperature 0.5 do compared with 1.0?
jd.m4.2.e: The logits are divided by the temperature. Less than 1 amplifies the differences.
jd.m4.2.o2: Sharpens the distribution: more probability to the top candidates
jd.m4.2.o4: Halves the length of the response
jd.m4.3.e: The number of candidates adapts: few when the model is confident, many when it is unsure.
jd.m4.3.o3: The smallest set of tokens whose probabilities together reach 0.9
jd.m4.4.q: 4. Why can’t all output tokens be computed in parallel during generation?
jd.m4.4.e: During training the whole text is known and everything is computed in one pass. During generation the next token does not exist until it has been drawn.
jd.m4.4.o1: The GPU has too little memory
jd.m4.4.o2: Each token depends on the previous one, which has to be sampled first
jd.m4.4.o3: Attention can only handle one position at a time
jd.m5.1.q: 1. What is the target for position t during pretraining?
jd.m5.1.e: The targets are the inputs shifted one step.
jd.m5.1.o1: The same token as at position t
jd.m5.1.o3: The last token in the sequence
jd.m5.2.q: 2. Why can training compute the loss for all positions in a single forward pass?
jd.m5.2.e: This is called teacher forcing. The mask means position t only sees 0..t even though everything sits in the same tensor.
jd.m5.2.o2: The whole sequence is known in advance, and the causal mask stops positions from seeing their answers
jd.m5.2.o3: The KV cache stores intermediate results
jd.m5.2.o4: Each position is run as its own batch
jd.m5.3.q: 3. Roughly how much memory per parameter does training with AdamW and mixed precision take?
jd.m5.3.e: Weight, gradient, fp32 copy and two Adam states. On top of that come activations for the backward pass.
jd.m5.4.q: 4. What sets a reasoning model apart from an ordinary one, architecturally?
jd.m5.4.e: The difference is in the weights. To an inference engine it is just more decode steps.
jd.m5.4.o2: It has a separate planning module
jd.m5.4.o3: Nothing; it is trained to write out a line of reasoning before the answer
jd.m6.1.q: 1. What limits the speed when a single sequence is decoded on a modern GPU?
jd.m6.1.e: Each step reads all the weights but computes only one row. The GPU waits for memory: memory-bound.
jd.m6.1.o2: How fast the weights can be read from memory
jd.m6.2.q: 2. What is stored in the KV cache?
jd.m6.2.e: Only keys and values. Queries, scores and MLP activations are computed and thrown away.
jd.m6.2.o1: The attention weights P for each step
jd.m6.2.o3: K and V for each position, in every layer and every KV head
jd.m6.2.o4: The whole residual stream for each position
jd.m6.3.q: 3. Why is it correct to reuse K and V for old positions?
jd.m6.3.e: It is exact, not an approximation. You saw it in the mini model: the logits come out the same with and without a cache.
jd.m6.3.o1: They change so little that the error is negligible
jd.m6.3.o2: The causal mask means a position is never affected by later tokens
jd.m6.3.o3: The model is retrained to tolerate it
jd.m6.4.q: 4. How much KV cache does one token take in Llama-3-8B with bf16?
jd.m6.5.q: 5. The decode batch goes from 1 to 16 sequences with short context. What happens?
jd.m6.5.e: The weights are read once per step regardless of batch size. The extra work per sequence is small.
jd.m6.5.o2: Each step takes almost the same time, so throughput becomes almost 16 times higher
jd.m6.5.o3: Nothing, the GPU runs them one at a time anyway
jd.m6.5.o4: The memory for the weights becomes 16 times larger
jd.m6.6.q: 6. What does TTFT mainly consist of?
jd.m6.6.e: The first token cannot arrive until the whole prompt has run through the model.
jd.m6.6.o2: Queue time plus prefill of the prompt
jd.m6.6.o4: The time to load the model
jd.m7.1.q: 1. An MoE model has 100 B parameters in total and 10 B active per token. How much GPU memory do the weights need in bf16?
jd.m7.1.e: All experts have to be in memory: 100 B · 2 bytes. The active parameters drive the compute, not the memory.
jd.m7.1.o4: It depends on the batch size
jd.m7.2.q: 2. What decides which experts a token is sent to?
jd.m7.2.e: The router is trained together with the rest. Each layer has its own.
jd.m7.2.o1: The topic of the token, from a fixed table
jd.m7.2.o2: A learned linear router per layer that scores from the token’s vector
jd.m7.3.q: 3. Which of these gives the smallest KV cache per token and layer (d_h = 128)?
jd.m7.3.e: MHA: 8,192 numbers, GQA-8: 2,048 numbers, MLA: 576 numbers.
jd.m7.3.o3: MLA with a latent vector of 576 numbers
jd.m7.4.q: 4. What does a long reasoning cost in an inference server?
jd.m7.4.e: Thinking tokens are ordinary output tokens. They take decode time and KV memory just like the answer.
jd.m7.4.o2: Many more decode steps and a growing KV cache
jd.m8.1.e: With blocks of 16 tokens allocated on demand, the waste is at most one partially filled block per sequence.
jd.m8.1.o1: That attention is quadratic in sequence length
jd.m8.1.o2: That KV memory was reserved in large contiguous chunks that mostly sat empty
jd.m8.1.o3: That the weights do not fit on one GPU
jd.m8.2.q: 2. What does a block table do?
jd.m8.2.e: The same idea as a page table in an operating system. The blocks do not have to sit next to each other.
jd.m8.2.o1: Maps a sequence of logical blocks to physical blocks in the pool
jd.m8.2.o3: Stores the hashes for the prefix cache
jd.m8.2.o4: Keeps track of which GPUs are free
jd.m8.3.q: 3. What does a hit in the prefix cache require?
jd.m8.3.e: Each block’s hash builds on the previous block’s hash. A single deviating token early on breaks the chain from there.
jd.m8.3.o3: The same tokens from the start of the prompt, in whole blocks
jd.m8.4.e: A slot that frees up is filled straight away by the next request in the queue.
jd.m8.4.o1: That the batch is decided anew in every step
jd.m8.4.o2: That all requests in a batch must finish at the same time
jd.m8.4.o3: That the GPU is never switched off
jd.m8.4.o4: That prompts are merged into one long sequence
jd.m8.5.q: 5. The startup log says: Maximum concurrency for 8,192 tokens per request: 47.50x. What does that mean?
jd.m8.5.e: The size of the KV pool in tokens divided by max-model-len. Shorter sequences mean more of them fit.
jd.m8.5.o1: The server is 47.5 times faster than a CPU
jd.m8.5.o2: The KV pool holds roughly 47 sequences that are all 8,192 tokens long
jd.m8.5.o3: At most 47 requests can be queued
jd.m8.5.o4: The batch size is locked to 47
jd.m8.6.q: 6. vllm:num_preemptions keeps climbing. What is the likely cause?
jd.m8.6.e: Lower max-num-seqs or max-model-len, use fp8 for the KV cache or add memory.
jd.m8.6.o2: The KV pool fills up, so requests are thrown out and recomputed
jd.m8.7.q: 7. Why does vLLM flatten the batch to [N_tokens, 4096]?
jd.m8.7.e: Matmuls do not care which request a row belongs to. Attention gets the boundaries via metadata.
jd.m8.7.o2: Requests have completely different token counts per step, and padding would compute on empty positions
jd.m8.7.o3: So that attention can mix requests
jd.m8.7.o4: PyTorch does not support three dimensions
jd.m9.1.q: 1. How do you find a direction for a concept in the residual stream?
jd.m9.1.e: A difference of means gives a vector [4096] that points from “without” toward “with”.
jd.m9.1.o1: By reading off the largest weight in each layer
jd.m9.1.o2: By taking the difference between the mean activations for examples with and without the concept
jd.m9.1.o4: By sorting the tokens by probability
jd.m9.2.q: 2. What does x ← x − (x · r̂) r̂ do?
jd.m9.2.e: It is a projection away from r̂. Afterwards x · r̂ = 0.
jd.m9.2.o2: Flips the vector to point the other way
jd.m9.2.o3: Removes the component along r̂ and leaves the rest untouched
jd.m9.3.q: 3. Which matrices change if the ablation is baked into the weights?
jd.m9.3.e: If nothing can write along r̂, the signal can never arise in the stream. No shape changes.
jd.m9.3.o3: Those that write to the residual stream: o_proj, down and embedding
jd.final.1.q: 1. Which order is correct for a forward pass?
jd.final.1.e: Text → ids → vectors → 32 layers → logits → new token.
jd.final.1.o1: Embedding → tokenizer → block → sampler → LM head
jd.final.1.o2: Tokenizer → embedding → block → LM head → sampler
jd.final.1.o3: Tokenizer → LM head → block → embedding → sampler
jd.final.1.o4: Sampler → tokenizer → embedding → block → LM head
jd.final.2.q: 2. Which tensor has shape [32, T, T] during prefill in Llama-3-8B?
jd.final.2.e: One T × T matrix per query head.
jd.final.2.o1: The KV cache in one layer
jd.final.3.q: 3. “Can you see which weights a question activates?” What is the best answer for a dense model?
jd.final.3.e: The weights are the program, the activations are the state. In MoE models, on the other hand, you can see which experts were chosen.
jd.final.3.o1: Yes, roughly 10% of the weights are activated per question
jd.final.3.o2: No, all weights are used every time; what varies, and what you can study, are the activations
jd.final.3.o3: Yes, but only in the last layers
jd.final.4.q: 4. What happens to the KV cache when a new token is generated?
jd.final.4.e: One row of K and one row of V per KV head and layer.
jd.final.4.o2: One new position is added in every layer
jd.final.4.o4: Nothing, it is fixed after prefill
jd.final.5.q: 5. Which is largest for Llama-3-8B in bf16?
jd.final.5.e: 128,000 · 128 KiB ≈ 16 GB, and the weights are ≈ 16 GB.
jd.final.5.o1: The weights are far larger than the KV cache for 128,000 tokens
jd.final.5.o2: The KV cache for 128,000 tokens is roughly as large as the weights
jd.final.5.o3: The KV cache is always negligible
jd.final.6.q: 6. The GPU shows low compute load while a single sequence decodes. Why?
jd.final.6.e: The fix is more sequences per step, not a faster GPU core.
jd.final.6.o2: Decode is memory-bound: the time goes into reading weights, not computing
jd.final.7.q: 7. Why does vLLM compute logits only for the last position in each sequence?
jd.final.7.e: Training needs every position. Generation needs only the last one.
jd.final.7.o1: The other positions have no vectors
jd.final.7.o2: Only that one predicts the next token; the rest would be T · V numbers for nothing
jd.final.7.o3: The LM head has no weights for other positions
jd.final.8.q: 8. Two requests share a 2,000-token system prompt. What does prefix caching save for the second one?
jd.final.8.e: 125 full blocks are reused. Only the rest of the prompt is prefilled.
jd.final.8.o1: Nothing, the cache only covers the same user
jd.final.8.o2: Prefill of the shared full blocks, that is almost the whole system prompt
jd.final.9.q: 9. Which statement about MoE is correct?
jd.final.9.e: Memory by the total, compute by the active ones. MoE replaces the MLP, not attention.
jd.final.9.o1: Only the active experts need to sit in GPU memory
jd.final.9.o2: All experts must sit in memory, but each token computes through only a few
jd.final.9.o3: The experts are split by topic by the developers
jd.final.10.q: 10. Why does speculative decoding pay off?
jd.final.10.e: Decode is memory-bound, so a few extra rows in the same pass are almost free.
jd.final.10.o1: The draft model is more accurate
jd.final.10.o2: Verifying several tokens in one pass costs almost as little as one regular decode step
jd.final.11.q: 11. What does TP = 2 mean for a model with 8 KV heads?
jd.final.11.e: Layers on different GPUs means pipeline parallelism. Full copies means data parallelism.
jd.final.11.o1: Each GPU holds the whole model
jd.final.11.o2: Each GPU holds half of every matrix and 4 KV heads; two all-reduces per layer
jd.final.11.o3: The layers are split: 16 on each GPU
jd.final.11.o4: The KV cache is duplicated on both
jd.final.12.q: 12. What changes in the model with a targeted ablation baked into the weights?
jd.final.12.e: That is why such a model runs in vLLM without any changes.
jd.final.12.o3: The contents of the matrices that write to the residual stream; all shapes are unchanged
jd.gloss.1.def: An intermediate value computed during a forward pass. Changes for every token, unlike weights.
jd.gloss.2.def: An operation where several GPUs sum their partial results so that all of them end up with the same tensor. Used twice per layer with tensor parallelism.
jd.gloss.3.def: The part of the block where each position fetches information from earlier positions, weighted by how well its query matches a key.
jd.gloss.4.def: The model generates one token at a time, and every new token becomes input to the next step.
jd.gloss.5.def: Several sequences processed in the same forward pass.
jd.gloss.6.def: 16-bit floating point. The standard format for weights in inference: 2 bytes per parameter.
jd.gloss.7.def: A chunk of KV memory for a fixed number of tokens, 16 by default in vLLM.
jd.gloss.8.def: A per-sequence list that maps logical blocks to physical blocks in the KV pool.
jd.gloss.9.def: Byte Pair Encoding. A method for building a vocabulary by merging common character pairs.
jd.gloss.10.def: A rule in attention that makes position i see only positions 0..i.
jd.gloss.11.def: A template that turns a list of messages into a single string with special tokens.
jd.gloss.12.def: A long prompt is split over several steps so that it does not block other requests.
jd.gloss.13.def: Speed is limited by the GPU’s compute power. Applies to prefill.
jd.gloss.14.def: The composition of the batch is decided afresh at every step.
jd.gloss.15.def: A recorded chain of GPU calls that is replayed in one go to reduce CPU overhead.
jd.gloss.16.def: The width of the residual stream. 4096 in Llama-3-8B.
jd.gloss.17.def: The phase where tokens are generated one at a time using the KV cache.
jd.gloss.18.def: A table with one vector per token. The first step: id → vector.
jd.gloss.19.def: A transformer with a single stack, where each token sees the tokens before it. The GPT and Llama families are built this way.
jd.gloss.20.def: The original placement of normalization: the stream itself is normalized after every addition.
jd.gloss.21.def: An architecture from 2017 in which attention does most of the work. The foundation of today’s language models.
jd.gloss.22.def: One of several parallel MLPs in an MoE layer.
jd.gloss.23.def: Number of floating-point operations. Roughly 2 per parameter and token in a forward pass.
jd.gloss.24.def: 8-bit floating point. Halves memory compared with bf16.
jd.gloss.25.def: Grouped-Query Attention. Several query heads share one KV head, which shrinks the KV cache.
jd.gloss.26.def: Sampling that always picks the most probable token. Equivalent to temperature 0.
jd.gloss.27.def: One of several parallel attention computations in a layer. 32 query heads in Llama-3-8B.
jd.gloss.28.def: Inter-token latency, time per output token. The time between two tokens in the response.
jd.gloss.29.def: A vector that describes what a position offers. Compared with queries. Stored in the KV cache.
jd.gloss.30.def: Saved keys and values for all previous positions, per layer. Lets decode compute only the new position.
jd.gloss.31.def: Storing weights with fewer bits, for example FP8 or int4.
jd.gloss.32.def: One round of attention plus MLP, with 7 weight matrices and 2 norm weights. Llama-3-8B has 32.
jd.gloss.33.def: Passing the residual stream from an intermediate layer through the final norm and LM head, to see what the model “thinks” at that point.
jd.gloss.34.def: A file (often safetensors) that maps tensor names to weights, for example model.layers.5.self_attn.q_proj.weight.
jd.gloss.35.def: One of the 14,336 detectors in an MLP layer: a column in each of W_gate and W_up, and a row in W_down.
jd.gloss.36.def: A single weight matrix that transforms a vector, for example q_proj. Called a “linear layer” in PyTorch.
jd.gloss.37.def: A linear classifier trained on activations to see whether a feature is linearly represented.
jd.gloss.38.def: The last matrix, [d, V], that turns a vector into logits. Also called unembedding.
jd.gloss.39.def: One number per token in the vocabulary, before softmax.
jd.gloss.40.def: Speed is limited by how fast data can be read from memory. Applies to decode.
jd.gloss.41.def: Multi-head Latent Attention. K and V are compressed into a latent vector that is cached.
jd.gloss.42.def: The part of the block that processes each position on its own. Also called feed-forward.
jd.gloss.43.def: Mixture of Experts. The MLP is replaced by many experts, and a router picks a few per token.
jd.gloss.44.def: vLLM’s way of storing the KV cache in blocks with a block table, similar to virtual memory.
jd.gloss.45.def: The layers are split across GPUs: the first ones on one, the later ones on the next.
jd.gloss.46.def: A request is thrown out of the batch when KV memory runs out and is recomputed later.
jd.gloss.47.def: The phase where the whole prompt runs through the model at once and the KV cache is filled.
jd.gloss.48.def: KV blocks for a shared prompt prefix are reused across requests.
jd.gloss.49.def: Normalization before attention and the MLP instead of after.
jd.gloss.50.def: A vector that describes what a position is looking for. Computed and thrown away at every step.
jd.gloss.51.def: The per-position vector that runs through all layers and that every layer adds to.
jd.gloss.52.def: Normalization that scales a vector so that its RMS becomes 1.
jd.gloss.53.def: Rotary Position Embedding. Q and K are rotated depending on position.
jd.gloss.54.def: A small linear matrix in an MoE layer that scores each expert.
jd.gloss.55.def: The size of a tensor along each axis, for example [T, 4096].
jd.gloss.56.def: SiLU is a smooth variant of ReLU. SwiGLU is the MLP variant where SiLU(gate) is multiplied by up.
jd.gloss.57.def: Per token: which slot in the KV pool its K and V should be written to.
jd.gloss.58.def: Turns numbers into probabilities that sum to 1.
jd.gloss.59.def: A token with a special role, for example the start of the sequence or the end of a turn.
jd.gloss.60.def: A cheap guess at several tokens is verified by the large model in a single pass.
jd.gloss.61.def: Adding a direction to the residual stream to influence behavior.
jd.gloss.62.def: Sampling constrained by a grammar so that the output always follows a format.
jd.gloss.63.def: The number that logits are divided by before softmax. A low value gives a sharper distribution.
jd.gloss.64.def: Every weight matrix is split across several GPUs.
jd.gloss.65.def: Tokens per second, summed over all requests.
jd.gloss.66.def: A piece of text with an id in the vocabulary. Roughly a short word or part of a word.
jd.gloss.67.def: Cuts away unlikely tokens before sampling: the best k, or the smallest set that reaches probability p.
jd.gloss.68.def: Time to first token. Queue time plus prefill.
jd.gloss.69.def: The vector a position passes on when it is picked in attention. Stored in the KV cache.
jd.gloss.70.def: A learned number in the model. Fixed after training and used for every token.
jd.gloss.71.def: The set of all tokens. 128,256 in Llama 3.
